prompt: A client sends `SET order:1002 paid` straight to a replica. What happens?

choices.text: The replica forwards it to the primary and answers `OK`
choices.why: Redis replicas do not forward; the client has to find the primary.

choices.text: It is refused with `READONLY`
choices.why: Right. A replica is read-only by default, so it cannot hold data its primary never saw.

choices.text: It is stored on the replica and copied back to the primary later
choices.why: Replication runs one way only, from primary to replica.

choices.text: It is queued until the replica is promoted
choices.why: Nothing queues it; the error comes at once.

prompt: The primary reports `master_repl_offset` 5000 and a replica reports `slave_repl_offset` 4200. What does that say?

choices.text: The replica has 800 bytes of writes it has not received yet
choices.why: Right. Equal offsets mean the replica has everything; the gap is how far behind it is.

choices.text: The replica has 800 keys fewer than the primary
choices.why: Offsets count bytes of the replication stream, not keys.

choices.text: The replica is 800 milliseconds behind
choices.why: The unit is bytes; lag in seconds is a separate field.

choices.text: The replica has disconnected and will need a full copy of the dataset when it returns
choices.why: A small gap is the normal state of an asynchronous replica.

prompt: Why is a replica not a backup?

choices.text: A replica cannot be read from
choices.why: It answered `GET` in the lesson.

choices.text: A replica keeps only the last hour of writes
choices.why: It holds the whole dataset.

choices.text: A mistake on the primary reaches every replica within milliseconds
choices.why: Right, a `FLUSHALL` included. A backup is a copy that a mistake does not reach: lesson 13's files, kept elsewhere.

choices.text: A replica stores its data in a format the primary cannot load back after a crash
choices.why: Same format; that is not the reason.

prompt: Why does the lesson run three Sentinels with a quorum of 2, rather than one?

choices.text: One Sentinel cannot tell a dead primary from its own lost link
choices.why: Right, and it would be a single point of failure. A majority that agrees is what makes a failover trustworthy.

choices.text: Each Sentinel watches one replica, and there are three servers
choices.why: Every Sentinel watches the whole set.

choices.text: A Sentinel can only promote a replica on its own machine
choices.why: It promotes over the network, any replica.

choices.text: Three Sentinels make failover three times faster
choices.why: Speed comes from `down-after-milliseconds`; more Sentinels add agreement, not speed.

prompt: With `sentinel down-after-milliseconds shop 5000`, how many seconds must the primary be silent before a Sentinel considers it down?
After a failover, the old primary `redis-1` is started again. What does it become?

choices.text: The primary again, because its name is in the Sentinel configuration
choices.why: Sentinel rewrote its file when the primary changed; the old name is history.

choices.text: A replica of the new primary, by Sentinel's instruction
choices.why: Right. Two primaries for one dataset is what failover must never produce.

choices.text: A second primary, until somebody demotes it by hand
choices.why: Sentinel reconfigured it as soon as it could reach it.

choices.text: Nothing: it refuses to start until its data is deleted
choices.why: It starts, and then resynchronises from the new primary.

prompt: An application is configured with `redis-1:6379` as its Redis address. Sentinel fails over to `redis-3`. What does the application see?
hint: Who knows that the primary moved?

choices.text: Nothing: Sentinel moves the address `redis-1` to the new server
choices.why: Sentinel moves the role, not names or addresses.

choices.text: Errors until `redis-1` returns, then `READONLY` errors on writes, because `redis-1` comes back as a replica
choices.why: Right. A client has to ask a Sentinel for the primary of `shop`, not hold an address.

choices.text: A short pause, then its writes go to `redis-3` on their own
choices.why: Nothing redirects a client that never asked Sentinel.

choices.text: A `MOVED` error pointing at `redis-3`
choices.why: `MOVED` is Redis Cluster's redirection; Sentinel has none.

prompt: Why does each Sentinel in the lesson get its own copy of `sentinel.conf`, in its own directory?

choices.text: Each Sentinel rewrites its file as it learns about replicas, other Sentinels and the primary
choices.why: Right. One shared file would be rewritten by three processes at once.

choices.text: Each file names a different primary to watch
choices.why: All three files are identical when they start: same `monitor` line.

choices.text: Docker cannot mount one file into three containers
choices.why: It can; the problem is three writers, not the mount.

choices.text: The quorum is counted by the number of files
choices.why: The quorum is the number in the `monitor` line.

prompt: In the lesson, order 2002 was written to the primary after it was cut off from the network, and answered `OK`. Where is it after the network heals?

choices.text: On the old primary only, which now disagrees with the others
choices.why: The old primary became a replica and flushed its data on the full resync.

choices.text: Nowhere
choices.why: Right. The promoted replica never had it, and the old primary threw it away when it rejoined.

choices.text: On every server, merged in when the old primary rejoined
choices.why: Redis does not merge two histories; the new primary's dataset wins whole.

choices.text: In the Sentinels' logs, from which it can be replayed
choices.why: Sentinels log events about servers, never data.

prompt: A client runs `SET order:2004 paid` and then `WAIT 1 2000`, which answers `0`. What is true of order 2004?

choices.text: It was rolled back, since no replica confirmed it
choices.why: `WAIT` undoes nothing; `GET` still found it on the primary.

choices.text: It is on the primary and on no replica, so a failover now would lose it
choices.why: Right. The application now knows the write is at risk, and can say so instead of confirming the order.

choices.text: It is safe: `WAIT` keeps retrying in the background until a replica has it
choices.why: `WAIT` only reports; replication carries on as before, and the partition stops it.

choices.text: It was refused with `NOREPLICAS`
choices.why: The `SET` answered `OK`; the refusal came later, once the lag passed 10 seconds.

prompt: A primary has `min-replicas-to-write 1` and `min-replicas-max-lag 10`. It is cut off from both replicas at 12:00:00. For at most about how many seconds can it go on accepting writes that will be lost?
hint: When does the primary start refusing?

prompt: A team lowers `min-replicas-max-lag` from 10 to 1 to shrink the window. What do they pay for it?

choices.text: Nothing: a lower lag is strictly safer
choices.why: Safer for consistency, and paid in availability.

choices.text: Every write now waits for a replica before answering
choices.why: Writes still answer at once; only the refusal rule changed.

choices.text: Sentinel fails over more often
choices.why: Sentinel's timing is `down-after-milliseconds`, a separate setting.

choices.text: The primary refuses writes during ordinary network hiccups too
choices.why: Right. A one-second gap in the replicas' acknowledgements is now enough to stop writes.

prompt: How many hash slots does Redis Cluster divide the key space into?
`redis-cli` without `-c` sends `SET product:KB-101 34990` to node 1 and gets `MOVED 14967 172.18.0.4:6379`. What happened to the write?

choices.text: Node 1 stored it and forwarded a copy to the owner
choices.why: Nodes do not forward commands; they tell the client where to go.

choices.text: Nothing was written; the client must send it to the node that owns slot 14967
choices.why: Right. With `-c`, `redis-cli` follows the redirection itself.

choices.text: It was written to slot 14967 on node 1, which from now on owns that slot and answers for it
choices.why: Slots move only by resharding, never because a client wrote to the wrong node.

choices.text: The cluster is broken and needs `--cluster fix`
choices.why: `MOVED` is the normal answer of a healthy cluster.

prompt: To keep `cart:ana:items` and `cart:ana:total` in one slot, the keys are renamed so that both contain `___cart:ana}`, and only that part is hashed.
A developer puts every customer's cart under the hash tag `{carts}` so that a Lua script can update any two carts together. What goes wrong as the shop grows?

choices.text: The script is refused with `CROSSSLOT`
choices.why: Every key is in one slot, so the script runs; that was the point.

choices.text: Every cart lands in one slot on one node, which takes all the load and memory
choices.why: Right. A hash tag that groups too much is the hot partition of lesson 3.

choices.text: Carts are copied to every node, multiplying memory by three
choices.why: A slot lives on one primary and its replica, not everywhere.

choices.text: The braces make the keys expire with the hash tag
choices.why: A hash tag only chooses the slot.

prompt: In the lesson, the node that owned `product:KB-101`'s slot was stopped. Who took over its slots, and with what?

choices.text: Its replica, promoted by the other primaries
choices.why: Right, with the data it had replicated. The price was still there; a write not yet replicated would not have been.

choices.text: A Sentinel, which promoted the nearest replica
choices.why: A cluster runs no Sentinel; its primaries vote.

choices.text: The other two primaries, which split its slots between them so that the load stays even
choices.why: Slots move to the replica; other primaries take none without a reshard.

choices.text: Nobody: those slots refuse every request until the stopped node is started again
choices.why: That happens only to slots with no replica left.

prompt: The shop's Redis holds a few gigabytes and one server handles its writes easily. It must survive the loss of a machine. Which fits?

choices.text: Redis Cluster with three primaries
choices.why: It buys capacity the shop does not need, and forbids multi-key operations across slots.

choices.text: A primary, two replicas and three Sentinels
choices.why: Right. High availability of a dataset that fits one machine is Sentinel's case.

choices.text: One Redis with the append-only file and `appendfsync always`
choices.why: It survives a restart, not the loss of its machine.

choices.text: A primary and one replica, failed over by hand
choices.why: It works only when somebody is awake to do it.

prompt: Match each property to Sentinel or Cluster.

pairs.left: clients ask for the primary of `shop`
acknowledged writes can be lost in a failover

prompt: Which of these stop working, or need changes, when an application moves from Sentinel to Cluster? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A Lua script that updates a customer's cart and a stock counter together
choices.why: Right. The two keys are in different slots unless tagged together.

choices.text: `SELECT 2` to keep test data apart
choices.why: Right. A cluster has database 0 only.

choices.text: `INCR` on a single counter
choices.why: One key is always in one slot.

choices.text: Reading a hash with `HGETALL`
choices.why: A hash is one key.

prompt: Put the lesson's lost write in order.
items: The primary is cut off from the network
The Sentinels agree it is down and promote a replica
The network heals and the old primary becomes a replica
A full resync flushes order 2002 from the old primary
trap: The promotion happens while the old primary is still accepting writes.

prompt: A payment must never be confirmed and then lost. Which arrangement does the lesson point to?

choices.text: Redis with Sentinel and `WAIT 2 1000` after every payment
choices.why: `WAIT` reports and does not prevent; a failover can still lose an acknowledged write.

choices.text: Redis Cluster, since each slot has its own replica
choices.why: Cluster replication is asynchronous too.

choices.text: A store that acknowledges only after a majority has the write, such as a MongoDB replica set with majority write concern
choices.why: Right. Redis can hand the work out; the record of a payment lives where acknowledgement means a majority.

choices.text: Redis with `min-replicas-max-lag 1`
choices.why: It shrinks the window to about a second; it does not close it.
